notes.claim: A jet engine takes air in at the front, raises its pressure with a compressor, burns fuel in it, and blasts the hot gas out of a nozzle at the back.
The forward push on the engine and aircraft is the reaction to the jets of gas shooting backwards.
Forces come in pairs: when one thing pushes on another, the second pushes back on the first, equally hard and in the opposite direction (Newton's third law).
A jet engine applies this directly: gas thrown backwards pushes the engine, and the aircraft, forwards.
Thrust equals the mass of air leaving each second times its exit speed, minus the mass arriving each second times its incoming speed; with equal flows that is mass flow times the speed added.
The air's path: drawn in at the front, pressurised by the compressor, burned with fuel, then expanded out through the nozzle.
The idealised cycle a gas turbine engine follows is called the Brayton (or Joule) cycle.
A turbofan has an extra turbine at the rear that drives the fan through its own shaft, separate from the core compressor and core turbine.
In a turbofan a large fan surrounds the core; adding the fan gives more thrust for nearly the same fuel burned by the core.
